title: Business failure and why new businesses are most at risk
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define business failure, trace its main causes - weak management, a changing environment, liquidity problems - and explain why a business's first years are its most dangerous.

blocks.heading: When a business fails
blocks.text: A business fails when it stops trading because it can no longer cover its costs. Failure has shades: an owner who closes a solvent shop to retire has made a choice, not a failure; insolvency - the state of being unable to pay debts as they fall due - is the harder edge. For a small business the consequences land on real people: the owner's savings and credit are gone, the workers lose their wages, suppliers are left unpaid and the local economy loses the trade.

blocks.heading: Why businesses fail
blocks.text:
Three causes account for most failures, and they feed one another. Weak management: the owner can make the product but cannot price it, keep records or watch the money - costs leak for months before anyone notices. A changing environment: a competitor opens across the road, a supplier's prices jump, a new road moves the trade away from the old site, or customers' tastes shift - the business that does not notice and adapt is outrun. Liquidity problems: the bills falling due cannot be paid, even though each sale may be profitable on paper - and profit and cash are not the same thing: profit is earned across a period while cash arrives on particular days; when cash fails, suppliers stop delivering, wages go unpaid and the doors close.

The causes compound: weak records hide the environment change, the unnoticed change drains the money, and the empty till ends the business.

blocks.heading: How a liquid failure happens
blocks.text: Watch a young catering firm in Walvis Bay take a contract to feed a construction site. Condition: it must buy N$8 000 of meat, flour and fuel now, pay wages of N$3 500 each Friday, and wait until the client pays at the end of the month. Mechanism: the outgoings land weekly while the income lands monthly, so the firm's cash drains in the gap; the next contract's stock cannot be bought, because the money that would buy it is promised elsewhere. Consequence: suppliers suspend delivery, the client hears of it and delays payment further, and the firm stops trading - profitable on every contract it ever served, because profit is earned when the meals are cooked while cash arrives when the client chooses to settle. The stakeholder cost lands on the cooks' wages and the owner's savings. The remedy is timing - a deposit, staged payments or a reserve kept back - arranged before the gap opens, not after.

blocks.heading: Why new businesses fail more often
blocks.text:
A new business starts without what an established one has accumulated. It has no customers who already buy, no trading record, no settled routines, thin reserves - and often a founder whose savings are all in. Its forecasts have never been tested against real customers, and it usually leans on one product, one location and one person's health, so a single shock hits everything at once. Suppliers typically want cash up front from a firm with no history, while an established rival enjoys a month to pay, so the young firm's costs arrive earlier than everyone else's. When the owner has staked personal savings, one bad month can end the venture, because there is no cushion behind the first mistake.

The pattern is not local: a two-person software start-up in Lisbon that lives on one client's late invoices fails by the same arithmetic. And the risk falls with each year survived: every year of trading builds the record, the reserves and the customer base that absorb the next shock - which is why the first years are the most dangerous.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 1.3.1's start-up support exists precisely because these years are the riskiest - grants and training schemes lower the cost and skill barriers that catch young firms out. Topic 5's cash-flow forecasting is the tool that warns a profitable business it is about to run out of money. Topic 6 names the external shocks - competition, taxes, the wider economy - that most often knock a firm over. And Topic 1.1's added value explains why a business with high added value can still fail: the gap must cover every other cost, and arrive on time.
